1:
Where this verse belongs is the first question, and two say it belongs to the chapter before. Gill reads it as set against Esau and his posterity, who held their land as lords and proprietors while Jacob and his seed held theirs as strangers, and thinks the sentence would close the preceding history better than open a new one — but Jacob dwelt, he would render it. Ellicott says the same outright: this is not the beginning of a section but the end of the generations of Esau, since we were told Esau went into a land away from his brother, then that he dwelt in Mount Seir, and now the necessary word about the other brother is added, the Hebrew using the same conjunction each time. Gill adds the Targum of Jonathan's paraphrase, that Jacob dwelt quietly — in tranquillity and safety, his brother being gone into another country, so that he stayed where his father had lived and died, in the land his blessing had given him. Clarke keeps to the margin's rendering, the land of his father's sojournings, and places it probably in the vale of Hebron.

Calvin turns the same contrast into a lesson about faith. By Esau's departure the land was left to Jacob as its sole possessor, and yet in appearance he did not obtain a single clod of it; contented with the bare sight of the country he exercised his faith, and Moses compares him expressly with a father who had been a stranger there all his life. Jacob was no small gainer by his brother's removal, but the Lord willed that the advantage be hidden from his eyes, that he might depend entirely on the promise.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why this generation begins where it does. The history of Isaac opened with the founding of his house at the birth of his sons; but Jacob was abroad when his sons were born and had not yet come into undisputed possession of his inheritance, so his own history starts with the return to his father's tent and his entry on the family lands, covering his life as patriarch of the house he founded. Through this stretch the sons stand in the foreground, Joseph and Judah above all — Joseph, they say, might be described as the moving principle of the story that follows — yet Jacob remains the head of the house and the centre round which the whole revolves. They divide the rest of his life at the removal to Egypt, the years in Canaan and the close in Goshen, and note that everything in the first part works toward the migration: directly by the sale of Joseph, indirectly by the alliance of Judah.

Henry marks the turn in the narrative. Moses has no more to say of the Edomites except as they cross Israel's path, and now applies himself closely to the story of Jacob's family — not a bare barren genealogy like Esau's but a memorable and useful history. That Jacob is still a sojourner with a father yet living gives Henry his text: we shall never be at home till we come to heaven. He runs ahead into the verses following, and two observations belong here because he makes them here. Joseph, though his father's darling, was not bred in idleness — those do not truly love their children who fail to inure them to business and labour, the fondling of children being with good reason called the spoiling of them, and those trained up to do nothing likely to be good for nothing. The father's love had causes, in a dear mother lately dead and a son who was the comfort of his old age, grave and discreet while still a child; but proclaiming it by a finer coat was imprudent, since paternal government must be impartial, and children notice a difference the moment it is made.
2:
A heading that promises a genealogy and delivers a story puzzles all of them. Gill reports Aben Ezra and Ben Melech taking the word for events rather than descents, though he prefers to read it back to the chapter where Jacob's sons were listed, Esau's genealogy being a parenthesis after which the history resumes. Clarke takes it for the history of the lives and actions of Jacob and his sons, since nothing genealogical follows, though the word may point back to the tables just given. Calvin makes it a record of events and not a pedigree: Moses enumerates no sons or grandsons but sets out the cause of the brothers' envy, as if to say that, having summed up Esau's line, he returns to his own history. Wesley says only that this is no barren genealogy like Esau's but a memorable and useful one. Ellicott alone reads the formula as a rule without exceptions: a man's generations are always the history of his descendants, as Adam's give the flood and Terah's the history of Abraham — so this one runs to the end of the book, the story of how Jacob's family was carried into Egypt through Joseph.

What the boy was doing among his brothers is read two ways. Ellicott renders the Hebrew as he was lad with the sons of Bilhah, and takes it that the youngest had to wait on the rest, as David minded the sheep while his brothers went to the feast; the sons were scattered in detachments across the country their cattle covered, and Joseph, brought up in Bilhah's tent after his mother died when he was about nine, would naturally go with her sons — who seem to have taken no special part in his sale. Clarke chases the English word instead, deriving lad from the Hebrew for a child and lass from a contraction of ladess, and disposing of the story that King James had it inserted, since it stands in Edmund Becke's Bible of 1549 and Coverdale's of 1535.

Of the evil report Clarke says the most useful thing: conjecture has been busy about what it was, but the text is perfectly silent, and all we can make of it is that it increased a hatred first raised by the father's partiality and afterwards by the dreams. Calvin reports the guess that some intolerable crime is meant, and prefers the reading that the boy complained of being vexed with his brothers' reproaches. He also asks a question nobody else raises — why only the handmaids' sons are named here, when Leah's are not spared afterwards. Reuben was milder and Judah his own mother's son, but Simon and Levi, being older, were probably the leaders; Calvin's suspicion is that sons of concubines would be quicker to envy, their servile descent exposing them to contempt.

The coat Keil and Delitzsch will not have painted. It was a long coat with sleeves reaching to wrists and ankles, such as noblemen and kings' daughters wore, not the coat of many colours Luther took from the Greek and Latin; and the boy was loved above the rest as born in his father's old age, the first-fruits of the beloved Rachel, Benjamin being hardly a year old. That partiality, they add, made the brothers unable to speak peaceably to him — unable so much as to ask him how he did. Calvin thinks the love itself unremarkable, since aged fathers commonly favour a late child; what he finds monstrous is that a coat and similar trifles should inflame men to plan a killing, and that they would not excuse in their father what they would not share. He notes the Chaldee's way round one difficulty — son of his old age rendered a wise son, a man in understanding while a boy in years — which would meet the objection that Benjamin was the later child.
3:
Gill grounds the preference in the boy himself — the firstborn of the beloved Rachel, a lovely youth of a beautiful aspect, promising, prudent and pious. Ellicott takes the phrase son of his old age for a chronological difficulty: Jacob was ninety-one when Joseph was born and eight or nine years older at Benjamin's birth, so on the common belief that he was only twenty years in Padan-aram the handmaids' four sons must have been about Joseph's age and Leah's last two younger still. The epithet becomes intelligible only if he waited twenty-seven years after his marriage with Rachel, which would leave a considerable interval — the son long looked for, whose birth had given him so great happiness, whereas his joy at Benjamin's coming was bought at the terrible price of the mother's death.

What the coat was divides them. Clarke renders it a garment made up of stripes of differently coloured cloth, and finds his parallel in the toga praetexta of Roman youth, white and striped or fringed with purple, worn until seventeen and then exchanged for the plain toga virilis; such vestures of distinction, he adds, are worn all over Persia, India and China still. Ellicott sets out both explanations, the long garment with sleeves or fringes and the patchwork of various colours, and prefers the second on the evidence of the tomb at Beni-Hassan, where a train of captive Jebusites appears in rich robes whose patterns seem produced by sewing together small pieces of different colours, as beautiful dresses are made in India of strips of crimson and purple. He will not follow those who take the dress for a formal designation of Joseph as head of the family in Reuben's room, on the supposition that it marked the priestly office borne by the firstborn: the point is doubtful, and it was Judah to whom Jacob gave the right of primogeniture. Wesley says only that it was probably significant of farther honours intended him.

Clarke will not let the partiality pass. It is no wonder the brethren envied, when the father had made the boy so distinguished an object of his love; the old fable of the ape that hugged her favourite cub to death through kindness was directed against just such fondness. How they perceived it Gill puts to his words, his looks, his gestures, and the coat that marked him off from the rest. On their being unable to speak peaceably Clarke corrects the English — it does not mean they were continually quarrelling with him, but that they could not speak peace to him, would not accost him in a friendly manner or even wish him well. The eastern salutation is shalom lecha among the Hebrews and salam among the Arabs; and because peace with those nations comprehends every blessing spiritual and temporal, they are careful not to give it to men they do not cordially wish well. An Arab or a Turk will hesitate to return the salam to a Christian, and the refusal counts in his own country as a mark of hostility, proof not merely that he does not wish you well but that he will do you an injury if he gets the chance — precisely the case here, so that the brothers felt themselves at liberty to take the first opportunity against him. Keil and Delitzsch add that the hatred was increased when the dreams came, the sheaves and then the sun, the moon and eleven stars pointing in an unmistakeable way to supremacy, the first over the brethren and the second over the whole house of Israel; the repetition seemed to establish the thing as certain, so that they hated him the more for his dreams and his words alike.
5:
Gill has him tell it in the simplicity of his heart, not understanding it or imagining there was any meaning in it, with no design to affront but as an amusement and for their diversion, there being something in it he might himself think ridiculous. Ellicott weighs the thing as revelation. Dreams as a rule do but arise from a mind wearied with overmuch business, or from other trivial causes; yet God uses them from time to time for providential purposes, and they are then described as a lower kind of prophecy. In Joseph's life they form the turning point, and it is to be noticed that while revelations were frequently made to Jacob, no such direct communication from God to man is recorded until the time of Moses. The utmost granted to Joseph was to dream dreams, and after this the children of Israel in Egypt were left entirely to natural laws and influences.

Henry and Wesley account for the gift by the boy who received it. Though now very young, about seventeen years old, he was pious and devout and well-inclined, and this fitted him for God's gracious discoveries of himself; and because a great deal of trouble lay before him, God gave him betimes this prospect of his advancement, to support and comfort him under the long and grievous troubles he was to be exercised with. Thus Christ had a joy set before him, Henry adds, and so have Christians; God has ways of preparing his people beforehand for the trials they cannot foresee, but which he has an eye to in the comforts with which he furnishes them.

Henry reads both dreams together and finds the second only a wider emblem of the first. The brethren's sheaves bowing to his intimate the very occasion on which the homage would be paid — their seeking to him for corn, their empty sheaves bowing to his full one; the sun and moon and eleven stars carry the same thing up to the whole family. Yet Joseph, he says, was more of a prophet than a politician, or he would have kept the telling to himself when he could not but know his brethren already hated him and that this would exasperate them further; and if he told it in simplicity, God directed it for their mortification. Then comes the observation Henry presses hardest: Joseph dreamed of his preferment, but he did not dream of his imprisonment — as many young people setting out in the world think of nothing but prosperity and pleasure, and never dream of trouble.

What the brethren made of it is, for Henry, an irony worth two lessons. They interpreted the dream truly, so that men who were enemies to its accomplishment became its expositors, as happened in Gideon's story and again when the chief priests perceived that Christ spoke of them; and while they committed crimes in order to defeat the thing, they were themselves the instruments of accomplishing it, exactly as the Jews, determined that Christ should not reign over them, made way by the crucifixion for the exaltation they had designed to prevent. The father he treats more gently. Jacob probably checked the boy in order to lessen the offence his brethren would take, and insinuated that it was an idle dream because the mother was brought into it who had been dead some time since — the sun, moon and stars signifying no more than a whole household that should have a dependence upon him. But he took notice of it more than he seemed to, and, like Mary, kept these things in his heart. Henry's warning is that the faith of God's people is often shaken by their misunderstanding the promises and then urging the improbabilities of the performance, while God is doing his own work and will do it whether we understand him aright or no.
6:
Calvin ascends higher than the quarrel and reads the dream as election. Moses has stated the first seeds of the enmity; now he shows that Joseph had been chosen by the wonderful purpose of God for great things, and told so in a dream, at which the hatred broke into madness. God revealed beforehand what he would do, so that it might afterwards be known that nothing had happened fortuitously, but that a celestial decree was carried by circuitous windings to its completion. It had been predicted to Abraham that his seed should be wanderers from Canaan, and this was the appointed method of the passage into Egypt: Joseph president there in a famine, bringing his father's whole house down to be fed. Nothing could have looked less likely. The sons conspire to kill the very man without whom they cannot be preserved; the minister of their salvation is thrown into a well, and afterwards into prison as into another sepulchre, where, neglected by the chief butler, he is left to rot. God accomplishes by such methods what he had purposed. Two things Calvin takes from it — that the Lord works by wonderful and unusual modes, and that he brings forth the salvation of his Church not from magnificent splendour but from death and the grave — and in Joseph, he says, a lively image of Christ is presented. The priority over his brethren was no wage of merit but the free gift of God, who ordained him chief of his mere good pleasure, that he might afterwards show kindness to them.

Of the sheaves themselves the notes are short. Gill prefers our version's modest hear, I pray you, to the reading of the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, hear now — lest he should forget a dream perhaps dreamt the night before. Ellicott makes stood upright the Hebrew for took its station, implying the position of chief, and infers that Jacob practised tillage regularly, as was usual at Haran too. Clarke thinks the dream too plain to need comment unless the grain points forward to the plenty in Egypt and the scarcity in Canaan that drove the brethren down for corn, where it was fulfilled to the letter. Calvin notices what the others pass over: the emblem is a farming one, and the sons were herdsmen with no harvest of their own to gather in. He takes the incongruity for a deliberate choice, showing that the prophecy was not founded on Joseph's present fortunes, and that the material of his dominion lay nowhere at hand, its cause to be sought elsewhere than at home.

Their answer was an accurate reading in a hostile mouth, and Gill says plainly that they understood the dream and its meaning better than he did. Wesley gives the scorn in its own form — shalt thou that art but one reign over us that are many, thou that art the youngest over us that are elder — and finds in it the world's standing quarrel with the reign of Christ, our Joseph, whom an unbelieving world cannot endure to think should reign over them. Calvin turns the episode into a warning for the elect: the paternal favour of God towards them is like a fan to excite the enmity of the world. That they fought in vain against God ought to have corrected the hatred: the man whose ruin their envy hurried them to seek was the man he had constituted chief. Perhaps the dream was meant also to alleviate the youth's trouble; their obstinacy only increased it. They were but too acute interpreters, and derided the dream as a fable because it was repugnant to their wishes — for the ill-disposed are often quick to perceive what the will of God is and, feeling no reverence, despise it. To that contumacy, Calvin ends, succeeds a stupor which destroys their former quick-sightedness.
9:
The second dream repeats the first, and everyone says so. Gill takes it as relating to the same subject, and given for the confirmation of it, the emblems only being different and more comprehensive; Clarke, who spends his note on a different question, pauses only to say that this dream is as clear as the preceding one. Ellicott makes the doubling a rule of this history — in Joseph's story the dreams are always double, though in the case of the chief butler and baker the interpretation was diverse. Calvin gives the reason for the change of emblem: the scope is the same, but to inspire greater confidence in the oracle God presents a figure from heaven, for the brethren had despised what was said about the sheaves, and now the Lord calls them to look upward, where his august Majesty shines forth. As for the objection that his mother was dead and could not come and bow down, Calvin thinks the sense plain without subterfuges, and the interpretation of certain Hebrews who refer the moon to Bilhah frigid: the sun and moon designate the head of the family on each side, so that in this figure Joseph sees himself reverenced by the whole house of his father.

Clarke feels the difficulty about the mother more sharply and offers three ways with it. Perhaps Jacob, in the very form of his question, meant to hint at the impossibility of the dream's being fulfilled, one of the chief actors in it being already dead. Or perhaps not: any one wife or concubine of Jacob was quite sufficient to fulfil that part of it. Some think, he adds, that Joseph may have had these dreams before Rachel died; but even were that the case, she certainly did not live to fulfil the part which appears to refer to herself. Clarke then asks a question nobody else raises. Why eleven stars? Was it merely to signify that his brothers might be represented by stars, or is there rather an allusion here to the Zodiac, his eleven brethren answering to eleven of the celestial signs and himself to the twelfth? He thinks it not an unnatural thought, since it is very likely that the heavens were already thus measured in Joseph's days, the zodiacal constellations having been distinguished among the eastern nations from time immemorial.
10:
Gill says he told it a second time in his brethren's hearing so that his father might pass judgment on it before them. Ellicott thinks the rebuke deserved on its face: in making the sun and moon bow down the dream seemed to violate the respect due to parents, and as Jacob probably took his son's dreams for the fruit of a fancy dwelling on self-exaltation, he rightly rebuked him — while nevertheless observing his saying. Wesley reads the reproof as tactical, given probably to lessen the offence his brethren would take, though he took notice of it more than he seemed to.

On the persons meant Ellicott is blunt. Rachel was certainly dead, since Joseph already had eleven brethren, and Leah never bowed before him either, for she died at Hebron. The enumeration of sun, moon and stars means Jacob, his wives and his children — the whole family, elders and juniors — a general phrase not to be interpreted too literally. He allows, though, that the handmaids, younger than either wife, may well have gone down with Jacob into Egypt, and that Bilhah had probably done a mother's part by Joseph after Rachel's death.

Calvin will not let the rebuke stand unexamined. If Jacob suspected vain ambition he rightly reproved his son; but if he knew God was the dream's author he ought not to have expostulated — and that he knew it may be inferred from his afterwards considering the thing seriously, Moses distinguishing between the sons, who breathed nothing but the virus of envy, and the father, who revolved in his own mind what it might mean. It ought to have occurred to him that Joseph, though under his authority, sustained a prophetic character. Calvin's conjecture is that, seeing his sons so malevolent, he feigned what he did not feel, unwilling to exasperate men who would not bear to be in subjection; and this method of pretending to be adverse to the truth, when we are trying to appease those who rage against it, is by no means approved by God. He ought rather to have exhorted them not to kick against the pricks, or at least to have said that if this were a common dream it deserved ridicule rather than anger, and if it came from God it was wicked to speak against it. It is even possible, Calvin allows, that the unsuitableness of the dream had struck the old man, since we know how hard it is to throw off every sense of superiority; and though he declines a little from the right course, his piety appears of no common order, his reverence for the oracle so easily prevailing over every other feeling.

The sons come off worse. Gill observes that all the father's precaution availed nothing: they suspected the dreams portended Joseph's pre-eminence over them, or at least filled his own mind with the expectation of it, and envied him for it. Calvin finds their obstinacy the worst thing here, and notices the contradiction in it: they despise the dream, yet are not made angry about nothing. Gladly would they have had their brother for a laughing-stock, but a secret sense of the Deity constrains them to feel there is something authentic in it, while a blind ferocity impels them to a resistance against God they never intended. Their case was the more censurable in that they not only rejected the oracle through hatred of subjection but were hostile to its messenger; and ours would be less excusable still, the doctrine of humility being now more clearly revealed and confirmed by the precious blood of Christ. If many at this day refuse the gospel and rise up against it, we need not be disturbed as by some new thing: the whole human race is infected with the disease of pride, and the gospel reduces all the glory of the flesh to nothing.
12:
Gill allows it was usual to drive flocks far for pasturage, Shechem being some sixty miles from Hebron where Jacob now dwelt; the marvel is the place itself. Jacob had bought a parcel of a field there, which gave them ground of their own to feed in; yet it was the town where they had destroyed all the males, and they might well have feared the neighbouring cities would rise and cut them off. Ellicott answers the fear from the same episode: the sons seem to have retained Shechem by right of their high-handed proceedings, Simeon and Levi having added the households they seized to their own retainers until they could resist any attack of the natives. What strikes Ellicott is what the distance implies — a great idea of Jacob's wealth and power, that he should send part of his cattle sixty miles from home.

Calvin reads the journey as an aggravation of what follows. Before treating the design of fratricide, Moses amplifies its atrocity by circumstances. The brother approaches them in the discharge of a duty, to make a fraternal inquiry after their state; he comes by his father's command and obeys without reluctance, as his answer shows; and though they had changed their place he spares no trouble till he finds them. Their cruelty was therefore something more than madness, since they did not shrink with horror from contriving the death of a brother so pious and humane. Nor does Moses relate without a purpose that a man met him wandering and told him they had gone to Dothan: the greater his diligence in that indefatigable pursuit, the less excusable were they who repaid it so.

Henry draws the obedience out as a pattern. Though the father's darling, he was made and was willing to be his father's servant, and how readily he waits the orders — here am I. Those best beloved by their parents should be the most obedient, and then the love is well returned. He objected neither the distance nor the danger, though he knew they hated him: it is a good lesson, learnt with difficulty and rarely practised, to love those who hate us. That he did not turn home when he missed them at Shechem, but sought diligently till he found them, shows he travelled out of love and not in obedience only.

What he met there Henry runs ahead to describe, fixing the moral on its deliberation. They conspired when they saw him afar off — not in a heat or on a sudden provocation, but from malice prepense and in cold blood; whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer, and the more of project and contrivance there is in a sin the worse it is, for it is bad to do evil but worse to devise it. Their scorn at the dreamer shows what fretted them, men who rage at God's counsels being bent on defeating them, and imagining a vain thing. In covering the deed with the tale of an evil beast they proved themselves worse than beasts, which do not prey on their own kind, whereas these were tearing a piece of themselves. Reuben had most reason of any to be jealous, being the firstborn entitled to the favours going to Joseph, yet he proves the best friend — God can raise up friends for his people even among their enemies, having all hearts in his hands; and Henry notes that the softness which had betrayed Reuben to uncleanness startled at the murder the fierceness of Simeon and Levi ran to. Through it all God was overruling to make Joseph an instrument to save much people alive; and in this Henry sees the type — the beloved Son sent out of his Father's bosom, coming to his own, who not only received him not but consulted against him: this is the heir, come let us kill him.
14:
The errand is a greeting, and Clarke will have it read so. Literally it is go and see the peace of thy brethren and the peace of the flock — go and see whether they are all in prosperity — which sends the reader back to what he had already said about the eastern salutation and the brothers who would not give it. Gill notices the courtesy of the wording, since the word may as well be rendered now, directly, immediately, which would agree better with a father's authority. Both Clarke and Ellicott find the reason for the anxiety in the same old crime: the sons were feeding on the parcel of ground bought from the Shechemites, where they had made that horrible slaughter, and the father might well fear the neighbouring tribes would form a confederacy and take vengeance. Ellicott adds the touch of character — they were far too fierce themselves to feel any such alarm, but Jacob was of a much more timid disposition.

On the geography the two go different ways. Ellicott locates the vale of Hebron by the pasture: the portion of Jacob's cattle that fed nearest home occupied the country immediately north of Hebron as far as the tower of Eder, though he would no doubt pitch his own tent as close as he could to his father's. Clarke reckons the distances instead — Shechem about sixty English miles from the vale of Hebron, and Dothan some eight miles beyond it — and then withdraws his own confidence in them, warning that all such calculations are very dubious, since we do not even know that the same place is intended, there being many proofs that different places went by the same names.

The stranger in the field draws out Gill's caution. Many of the Jewish writers say this was an angel, and Gabriel at that, in the likeness of a man; Aben Ezra makes him a traveller met on the road; but Gill prefers what Schimidt observes, that it was some man at work in the field who came upon him and took notice of him. He also supposes Joseph must have described his brethren and said whose they were, or the man could not have known whom he meant, and Joseph would never have made his request. Ellicott finishes the journey. Dothan lay twelve miles north of Shechem in a small but fertile valley, and is famous as the place where Elisha struck the Syrian army with blindness; the sons had exhausted the produce of the larger plain round Shechem and moved northward for feed. Not finding them, Joseph did not know where to go, and wandered about in the field, the open downs, until someone could inform him — whereas, Ellicott remarks, had he been a practised hunter like Esau he would have followed them by the tracks of the cattle.
18:
They knew him at that distance, Gill says, by his stature, his gesture or manner of walking, and above all by the coat of various colours he now had on. Wesley marks only the coolness of it: not in a heat or upon a sudden provocation, but from malice propense and in cold blood. The name they gave him is a title — Clarke and Ellicott both render it lord or master of dreams, a form of speech conveying great contempt. Gill follows the Targum of Jonathan in putting the words into the mouths of Simeon and Levi, men so hot and bloody minded, as the affair of Shechem showed; and he suspects this is why Joseph afterwards, as governor of Egypt, took Simeon and bound him — a just retaliation for the advice to cast him into a pit.

Calvin is severest here, and begins by praising Moses for the severity. So far from sparing his own family's fame, he brands its chiefs with a mark of eternal infamy and exposes them to the execration of all nations; profane history has nothing like nine brethren conspiring against an innocent youth and pouncing on him like wild beasts. What is worse than the fury is the contempt of God underneath it. Why insult the unhappy youth, except that a celestial oracle had called him to an unexpected dignity? They proclaim their own baseness by confessing that the cause was his having dreamed, as if that were an inexpiable offence; and if they are indignant at the dreams, why not rather wage war with God? Not daring to assail him directly, they wrap themselves in clouds, that, losing sight of God, they may vent their fury on their brother. The pretext they invent is of a piece with it. It never enters their mind that what is hidden from men cannot escape the eyes of God — so stupid is hypocrisy, which flees the world's disgrace and is careless of the judgment above it; the inward judge convicts, and they confirm themselves in impudence only that the disgrace may not appear. As if the truth of God could be subverted by the death of one man, they boast they will have their wish when their brother is killed and his dreams come to nothing. Turbulent envy drives them headlong to fight against God — and God will always find a way through the most profound abyss to the accomplishment of what he has decreed.

What they meant to throw him into Ellicott explains: one of the pits, cisterns dug to catch and preserve the rain, dry in summer, deep and narrow at the top, so that a man cast in would have little chance of escape. Clarke passes the pit for indignation at the talk around it: what unprincipled savages, to speak so coolly of imbruing their hands in an innocent brother's blood — and how necessary a divine revelation is to show man what God hates and loves, ferocious cruelty being the chief characteristic of nations that do not receive the law at his mouth. Calvin closes on the comfort. God's special favour had raised Joseph to the highest dignity, but only in a dream, which their wicked scorn ridiculed, and now a conspiracy nearly kills him: the promise that exalted him almost plunges him into the grave. So it goes with those who have received the gratuitous adoption of God amid many sorrows, for from the time Christ gathers us into his flock we are permitted to be cast down until we seem nearer hell than heaven. Let Joseph's example be fixed in our minds, Calvin says, that we be not disquieted when many crosses spring from the very root of God's favour; for in him was adumbrated what was afterwards exhibited in Christ, the Head of the Church, that every member might form itself to his example.
21:
Gill supposes Reuben overheard what was said without being in the consultation — perhaps Simeon and Levi did not want the elder brother in the debate, knowing his temper more mild and gentle and fearing he would overrule matters against them; or he was at some distance and entirely absent, and their intention was reported to him afterwards by one of them.

That the rescue should come from this man is what the others dwell on. Clarke grants he was a transgressor of no ordinary magnitude, if the earlier verse is taken according to the letter, yet his bosom was not the habitation of cruelty: he determined, if possible, to save his brother from death and deliver him safely to his father, with whose fondness for the boy he was sufficiently acquainted. Clarke has no patience, though, with the embellishment of the scene. Josephus, in his usual way, puts a long flourishing speech into Reuben's mouth on the occasion, spoken to dissuade the brethren from their barbarous purpose; but as it is totally unfounded, it is worthy of no regard.

Calvin makes the same contrast sharper, and thinks it worth observing by whose care Joseph was preserved while the rest were hastening to shed his blood. In one affair Reuben was the most wicked of them all, when he defiled his father's couch, and that unbridled lust, involving other vices, was the sign of a depraved nature; yet now, suddenly, he alone has regard to piety, and, mindful of fraternal duty, dissolves the impious conspiracy. Whether he was seeking some means of compensation, for the sake of which he might be restored to his father's favour, Calvin leaves uncertain; but since Moses declares his intention was to restore the boy in safety, the conjecture is probable that he thought his brother's life a sufficient price to reconcile his father's mind to himself. However that may be, the humanity he showed in attempting the deliverance is proof that he was not abandoned to every kind of wickedness — and perhaps God, by this testimony of his penitence, designed in some degree to lessen his former disgrace. Whence we are taught, Calvin says, that the characters of men are not to be estimated by a single act, however atrocious, so as to cause us to despair of their salvation.

Wesley reads the proposal itself as the double thing it was: one his brothers thought would effectually destroy Joseph, and one he designed should answer his own intention of rescuing him out of their hands, probably hoping by it to recover his father's favour, which he had lately lost. And the whole of it, Wesley adds, shows that God can raise up friends for his people even among their enemies.
22:
What Reuben said Gill reads against the original law: shed no blood — innocent blood, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, a brother's blood, the blood of one who had done nothing for which it should be shed, and which would bring vengeance on them. Ellicott thinks he pointed to some cistern in the desolate region girding the little valley of Dothan, and reminds us from a later chapter that Joseph begged hard for mercy and to be spared so painful a death, and that his brothers would not hear. Keil and Delitzsch put the outcome in a sentence: Reuben had indeed saved Joseph's life by his proposal, but his intention of sending him back to his father was frustrated.

Calvin will not let the compromise pass for mercy. The pious fallacy he descended to proves how vehemently the rage of his brethren was burning, since he dared neither openly oppose nor dissuade them, seeing that no reasons would soften them. Nor does their consenting extenuate the cruelty, as though they were disposed to clemency: better the boy should die at once by their hands than perish by slow hunger in the pit, the most cruel kind of punishment. Their gross hypocrisy is rather what should be noticed: they think themselves free from crime if only they do not stain their hands with blood, as if it made any difference whether they ran him through with a sword or suffocated him. When the Lord by Isaiah accuses the Jews of having hands full of blood, he does not mean that they were assassins, but calls them bloody because they did not spare their suffering brethren; and the sons of Jacob are nothing better, casting their brother alive under ground to contend in vain with death and perish after protracted torments, and choosing a pit in the desert from which no mortal could hear his dying cry, though his sighing would ascend even to heaven. It was a barbarous thought that they had not touched his life so long as they did not imbrue their hands in his blood, the death they meant by hunger being no less violent. Reuben accommodated his language to their brutal conceptions, deeming it enough to repress their impetuosity by any artifice for the present.

Ellicott turns from the pit to what the history has always been taken to mean. Joseph is nowhere in Scripture called a type of Christ, yet the Old Testament is so full of events which reappear in the Gospel narrative that the Fathers never hesitated to regard him so — the innocent delivered to death, but raised thence to glory. He borrows Pascal's summary of the resemblances: his father's love for him, his being sent to see after the peace of his brethren, their conspiring against him, his sale for twenty pieces of silver, his rising from humiliation to be the lord and saviour of those who had wronged him, and of the world besides; and as he was in prison with two malefactors, one delivered and one punished, so our Lord was crucified between two thieves, one saved and one left to his condemnation. The history is also, Ellicott says, a vindication of God's providential dealings with men. Joseph is innocent and pure in life, yet wronged again and again, and every wrong was but a step in the pathway of his exaltation. Nor does his life begin and end in himself: noble minds care little for personal suffering if amelioration for the world springs from their pain, and on this man a great future depended. His descent into Egypt was not only for the preservation of the people there, but an essential condition of the forming of the Jewish Church; for in Egypt alone could Israel have multiplied into a nation fit to be the depositaries of God's law, and to grow into a church of prophets.
23:
Gill notes what came just before the violence: Joseph had reached the very place where they were, asked after their welfare in a kind and obliging manner, and told them of the father's concern that sent him. Then the coat came off. Clarke supposes a practical reason for taking it: so that if ever found he might not be discerned to be a person of distinction, and no inquiry made about him. Henry sees only the spite: each striving to seize the envied coat, they degraded him in imagination from the birthright, of which perhaps this was the badge, grieving him, affronting their father, and making themselves sport while they insulted over him — now, Joseph, where is the fine coat? So, he adds, was our Lord Jesus stripped of his seamless coat, and so have his suffering saints been divested of their privileges and honours and then made the off-scouring of all things.

Calvin reports the guess that lies behind Henry's badge and declines it. Some supposed the coat belonged of right to the firstborn, so that Reuben was entitled to it until his misconduct forfeited it, and that Jacob transferred both it and the primogeniture to the eldest son of his best-loved wife — which, if true, would make Reuben's conduct here more generous than it appears. The objection is that Jacob is said to have made the coat for Joseph, not merely to have given it to him. What Calvin is certain of is that these men were full of fictions and lies. They strip their brother carelessly and feel no dread at casting him with their own hands into a pit where hunger worse than ten swords might consume him, because they hope the crime will be concealed, and because his clothes carried home would raise no suspicion, their father being sure to believe he had been torn by a wild beast. Conscience is indeed the fountain of modesty; but Satan so soothes those he has caught in his snares that the conscience which ought to have cited them before the bar of God only hardens them; having found subterfuges, they break out more audaciously, as if whatever escapes the eyes of men might be committed with impunity. It is a reprobate sense, he says, withheld from a daring attempt only by fear of the shame of men while the fear of divine judgment is trodden under foot; and the fault of paying more honour to men than to God is far too common. The repetition of the word for the coat he takes for emphasis: this mark of the father's love could not mollify their minds.

The pit itself Gill identifies as the very one Reuben had pointed to, whose counsel they gladly took and readily executed, supposing he meant the same thing they did — starving him to death. Henry says they went about to starve him, throwing him into a dry pit to perish with hunger and cold, so cruel were their tender mercies; where envy reigns pity is banished and humanity itself forgotten, and malice is so full of deadly poison that the more barbarous a thing is the more grateful it becomes. He fills in from the later chapter what this verse omits. Joseph begged for his life in the anguish of his soul, entreating by every imaginable endearment that they would be content with his coat and spare him, pleading innocence, relation, affection, submission, weeping and making supplication, all in vain; Reuben alone relented and interceded, and could not save him from the horrible pit where they had resolved he should die by degrees and be buried alive. Is this he, Henry asks, to whom his brethren must do homage? There he leaves the lesson: God's providences often seem to contradict his purposes at the very moment when they are serving them, and working at a distance toward their accomplishment.
25:
The meal is what appals them. Gill has them not at all concerned at what they had done, nor grieved for Joseph's affliction, but glad they had got him into their hands and were likely to be rid of him. Wesley reads the appetite as a verdict on the conscience: they felt no remorse, which if they had would have spoiled their stomach to their meat; a great force put upon conscience commonly stupefies it, depriving it for the time of sense and speech. Every act, Clarke says, is perfectly in character, describing forcibly the brutish nature of their ruthless souls. Calvin calls it an astonishing barbarity that they could quietly feast while in intention guilty of a brother's death, since even the worst men are commonly afraid after a crime; and because the patriarchs fell into such insensibility, let us fear the same lethargy.

The caravan draws out the antiquarians. Clarke supposes a company of different tribes travelling together for safety, of which Ishmaelites and Midianites made the chief; the Chaldee calls them Arabians, from a root meaning to mingle, and the Jerusalem Targum Sarkin, what we term Saracens; the Persian, he thinks, gives the true sense — a caravan of Ishmaelite Arabs came. Ellicott traces the road: Dothan lay on the great caravan line by which the products of India and Western Asia reached Egypt, the route running north-westward round the Arabian desert, over the Euphrates, from Tadmor to Gilead, and over the Jordan at Beisan. On the shifting names he is firm. For Ishmeelites we have Midianites later and Medanites at the chapter's close, while the Targum and Syriac read Arabs. Midian was Abraham's son by Keturah and Ishmael his son by Hagar, but probably these merchants descended from neither by blood, belonging rather to some branch of the Canaanites, the great traders of antiquity whom Ishmael and Midian had subdued. The Jewish interpreters, reduced to great straits, even assert that Joseph was sold three times; really the three are one and the same, the names being borne only politically.

The wares Ellicott identifies in turn: the spicery probably gum tragacanth, though some think storax; the balm the resin of the balsamodendron Gileadense, abundant in Gilead and much used for healing wounds; the myrrh certainly ladanum, gum of the cistus rose — all products of Palestine valued in Egypt, which is why Jacob afterwards sent them as a present to the governor.

Calvin sees in the caravan the admirable progress of God's counsel. Joseph had already passed through a double death, and now, as if by a third, is beyond all expectation rescued from the grave — for what was it less than death to be sold as a slave to foreigners? His condition was made worse by the chance, since Reuben would secretly have drawn him out and brought him back to his father, whereas now he is dragged to a distant part of the earth without hope of return; yet this was the secret turn by which God meant to raise him on high, the event showing how much better it was that he be led far from his family than remain in safety at home. Judah's speech has somewhat more reason in it, since he ingenuously confesses they would be guilty of homicide if they let him perish: what gain is it if his blood be covered, when our hands will nevertheless be polluted? Their fury was by then abating: outrageous perfidy to sell a brother to strangers, but something to send him away alive, that he might at least be nourished as a slave. What Judah says of his brother, Calvin ends, the Lord by the prophet extends to the whole human race: whenever depraved lust impels to unjust violence, let us remember the sacred bond binding society together, for a man cannot injure men without becoming an enemy to his own flesh.
26:
Gill makes the proposal opportunistic, and dates it to the moment the caravan came into view: it was in sight of the Ishmaelites that the thought came into Judah's mind to get Joseph sold to them, so that the scheme was both conceived and closed while the merchants were passing. Wesley puts the arithmetic of it plainly — what profit is it if we slay our brother? It will be less guilt and more gain to sell him; and they all agreed to it. From the price he takes the comparison the whole tradition has taken: as Joseph was sold by the contrivance of Judah for twenty pieces of silver, so was our Lord Jesus for thirty, and by one of the same name too, Judas.

Reuben's absence at the moment of sale is what both Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch fasten on. Wesley supposes he had gone away from his brethren intending to come round some other way to the pit and help Joseph out of it — a kind project, but had it taken effect, what had become of God's purpose concerning his preferment in Egypt? There are many devices of the enemies of God's people to destroy them and of their friends to help them, and both are perhaps disappointed, as these were; but the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand. Keil and Delitzsch read the absence from the brothers' side, and less charitably: the business was settled while he was away, probably because they suspected that he intended a rescue, so that the one man who meant to save him was the one man not consulted.

What he said on returning both take at its plainest. He thought himself undone because the child was sold, Wesley says, and being the eldest could expect his father to require an account of him — I, whither shall I go? Keil and Delitzsch call the rending of his clothes a sign of intense grief on the part of the natural man, and paraphrase the cry as a question about the reckoning: the boy is no more, and how shall I account to his father for his disappearance? The brothers were at no loss for an answer of their own, dipping the coat in the blood of a goat. And the irony Wesley leaves the reader with is that Reuben had it exactly backwards: it proved that they would all have been undone if Joseph had not been sold.
27:
Gill gives the motive of the sale in one line: sell him for a slave, and that will defeat his dream — for as these merchants were going down to Egypt, he would be far enough off, and there would be no probability of his ever being lord over them. On the two names Gill sees no problem, taking Midianites and Ishmaelites for the same people: near neighbours who joined together in merchandise and travelled in company for greater safety, mixing also in their habitations and marriages, so that they are sometimes called the one and sometimes the other, and are called Arabians by the Targums and by Josephus, which signifies a mixed people.

Calvin cannot dismiss it so easily, since Midian was Abraham's son by Keturah and his sons therefore distinct from Ishmael's, and Moses has not put down the different names thoughtlessly. Some, he reports, think Joseph was twice sold in the same place. It might be better explained by supposing the passing caravan made up of both, the Ishmaelites forming the larger and more conspicuous part and so giving their name to the whole, while the actual purchasers were the Midianitish merchants among them. Calvin's own reading is different again: Joseph was exposed for sale to any who chose, and the purchase being declined by the Midianites, he was sold to the Ishmaelites. The buyers, he adds, might justly have suspected the sellers of having stolen him, but the desire of gain prevented inquiry; and though they probably asked on the journey who he was, they did not set such value on their common origin as to forgo a profit. From the merchants themselves Calvin draws a lesson about the two seeds. From Abraham's sons after the flesh a posterity so great was propagated that from both proceeded traders in various places, while the part of his seed the Lord had chosen to himself was still small; for the children of this world, like premature fruit, quickly reach the greatest wealth and the summit of happiness, whereas the Church, slowly creeping through the greatest difficulties, scarcely attains in a long time to the condition of mediocrity.

The price is reckoned three ways. Clarke thinks this the first instance on record of selling a man for a slave, though the practice doubtless began long before; the Anglo-Saxon renders it thirty pence, and where our translators supply pieces the Persian has miskal, probably intended for a shekel — which at three shillings each would make about three pounds sterling. He sets a modern figure beside it: he had known a whole cargo of slaves, eight hundred and thirteen of them, bought by a slave captain in Bonny river in Africa at an average of six pounds each, and paid for in guns, gunpowder and trinkets. Since only nine of the brethren were present, he works out that each had more than two shekels as his share in this most infamous transaction. Ellicott measures the sum against the law instead: twenty shekels is reckoned in Leviticus the average worth of a male slave under twenty, about two pounds ten shillings of our money, though silver was of far greater value then than it is now.
29:
Reuben's absence has been made into a difficulty, and Ellicott thinks it really confirms the truth of the narrative. The difficulty arises solely from supposing that the brothers sat down to eat bread immediately after casting Joseph into the pit, an act well described as most cold-blooded; but they were not actually guilty of that, for what the narrative says is that they were having their evening meal when the caravan came in sight. Between the casting in and the meal Reuben had apparently gone a long round to fetch in the more distant cattle, and probably remained away as long as possible, in order to be sure his brethren would be at their dinner when he returned — hoping to reach the cistern alone, rescue Joseph, and send him away home before the rest could interfere. So rightly understood, Ellicott says, it is a proof of the trustworthiness of the history. Clarke observes only that he was absent when the caravan passed by, to whom the others had sold him. Gill supposes he had pretended to go somewhere on business, meaning to take a circuit and come to the pit and deliver his brother and go home with him to his father; and he reports the Jewish account that Reuben departed and sat down on a certain mountain so as to descend in the night and take Joseph out, coming down accordingly and not finding him — as Josephus too makes it night when he came to the pit, calling to Joseph and, getting no answer, suspecting that he had been killed.

What he said on finding the pit empty Clarke will not translate, observing only that the words in the original are very plaintive. Gill has him return to his brethren suspecting that they had taken him and killed him after their first design, since he had not been with them when they proposed the sale and made it. Calvin reads the whole manoeuvre as a secret kindness overtaken by events. Reuben stole away under pretence of some other business, so that, unknown to them all, he might restore his brother, drawn out of the pit, to his father; and there is no wonder that he was anticipated, when he had taken his course in a different direction from theirs, intending to reach the pit by a circuitous path. Only now, having lost all hope, does he unfold to his brethren the intention he had not dared to confess before, lest the boy should be immediately murdered. Keil and Delitzsch add the one fact that none of the brothers knew: while the father was mourning, Joseph was being sold by the Midianites to Potiphar.
31:
Gill draws two things from the taking of it. Reuben, told what they had done and willing to make the best of it, joined the scheme; and since they had the coat to dip, it appears that when they drew Joseph out of the pit they did not put it on him, but sold him naked. Ellicott corrects the picture of the animal — the Hebrew is a full grown he-goat, not a kid — and passes on Maimonides' conjecture that he-goats were so often used for sin-offerings under the law in order to remind Israel of this great sin of their patriarchs. Calvin thinks the coat was carried by servants not accessory to the crime, since the sons and daughters are said soon afterwards to have come and consoled him.

Henry gives the deception two purposes. The first was to clear themselves, for we have all learned of Adam to cover our transgression, and when the devil has taught men one sin he teaches them to conceal it with another — theft and murder with lying and perjury — though he that covers his sin shall not prosper long. They kept counsel for a time, but the villany came to light at last. The second was to grieve their father, contrived to be revenged on him for his distinguishing love. They sent the coat of many colours with one colour more than it had had, a bloody colour, and Jacob must be scornfully asked whether this were his son's coat; so the badge of his honour became the discovery of his fate. Love is always apt to fear the worst concerning the person beloved, Henry says; there is a love that casteth out fear, but that is a perfect love.

He asks those who know a parent's heart to put their souls into his soul's stead. Sleeping or waking he sees the beast setting upon Joseph and hears his piteous shrieks, and grows chill fancying how it tore him limb from limb and left no remains but the coat to carry the tidings; and it added no little to the grief that he had sent the boy alone, so that he looks on himself as accessory to his death. The comforters Henry treats with contempt: had they really wished to comfort him they might have done it by telling the truth, that Joseph was alive and could be ransomed; he wonders their countenances did not betray them, the heart being strangely hardened by the deceitfulness of sin. From the whole he warns that we often perplex ourselves with imaginary troubles, when sometimes there needs no more to comfort us than to undeceive us.

Calvin finds two lessons in the same scene. The first is against the brothers: whatever they intended, their wickedness drove them to inflict a deadly wound on their father's mind — all the profit hypocrites gain by their disguises being that, wishing to escape one fault, they add sin to sin. The second is against Jacob, and he does not soften it. It is a wonder that a man tried in so many ways, and always coming forth a conqueror, should now sink under grief — absurd that his son's death should cost him greater sorrow than the pollution of his wife, the slaughter of the Shechemites and the defilement of his daughter. Where was the strength by which he had prevailed even over the angel? The disposition to mourn teaches us, Calvin says, that no one is endued with such heroic virtue as to be exempt from that infirmity of the flesh which betrays itself even in little things; whence men long accustomed to the cross, who like veterans ought bravely to bear up against every attack, fall like young recruits in a slight skirmish. Who among us may not fear for himself, when we see holy Jacob faint after so many proofs of patience?
32:
How the coat reached the father is a small question the commentators take seriously. Gill has it sent by the hand of a messenger: the Targum of Jonathan names the sons of Zilpah and Bilhah, but more probably some of their servants, whom the brothers instructed what to say, not caring to appear in person at first lest the commotion and confusion they would be thrown into at their father's distress should lead on to a discovery of the whole affair. Ellicott reads the Hebrew the same way — they caused it to go, that is, sent it by the hand of a messenger — and gives the same reason, that they were unwilling to see the first burst of their father's agony; the words that follow, he notes, were what the messenger was charged to say. Clarke needs only one sentence for the whole manoeuvre: what deliberate cruelty, to torture the feelings of their aged father and thus harrow up his soul.

On the recognition Gill asks the reader to hear the verse rather than parse it. Jacob took the coat and examined it and was soon well assured whose it was; and if the words are read without the supplement, the pathos appears the greater — my son's coat! — so that one should think with what a beating heart, what trembling limbs, what wringing of hands, what flowing eyes and faltering speech he spoke it. Clarke supplies what made the inference so quick. It is likely Jacob judged from the lacerated state of the garment, which the brothers, the better to cover their wickedness, had not only besmeared with the goat's blood but probably reduced to tatters. And what must a father's heart have felt in such a case? As this coat is rent, so is the body of my beloved son rent in pieces — and Jacob rent his clothes.

Of the mourning Gill says only that the rending was expressive of his grief for a son he supposed dead. Ellicott measures its length instead. Jacob mourned not merely during the usual period but so long as to move even the hearts of those who had wronged him, for not only his daughters but all his sons rose up to comfort him; and how long and how intense the sorrow was may be gathered from what is said of it much later, when the news came that Joseph was alive. Probably, Ellicott adds, he had several daughters by Leah and by the two handmaidens, Dinah alone being mentioned by name because two of her brothers forfeited the birthright by the cruelty with which they avenged her wrong; the daughters are named again among those who went down into Egypt.
35:
Who the comforters were is a difficulty Gill will not settle. His sons acted a most hypocritical part; as for his daughters, Jacob had but one that we read of. The Targum of Jonathan makes them his sons' wives, though it is a question whether any of the sons were yet married, the eldest being not more than twenty-four; and the Jews hold that a twin daughter was born with each of his sons. They came to condole with him and entreat him not to give way to excessive sorrow. Clarke allows the sons' wives may be included, then turns on them: what hypocrisy to comfort him for the death of a son they knew was alive, and what cruelty to torture their aged father when there was no ground for it.

Ellicott takes up the word Jacob used for his destination — Sheol, which like the Greek Hades means the place of departed spirits — and notes that on his own supposition it can hardly be the tomb: believing Joseph devoured and unburied, he could not go down into the grave unto his son. Wesley reads the refusal as a resolution to go down to the grave mourning, and adds the maxim: great affection to any creature does but prepare us for the greater affliction when it is removed or embittered, inordinate love commonly ending in immoderate grief.

Calvin measures the burden of the grief by the gathering: that they rose up implies a common deliberation, they having agreed to come because necessity urged them. Hence appears how vast is the innate dissimulation of men, for the sons assume a character by no means suitable to them and perform an office of piety from which their minds are alien. Had they had respect unto God they would have acknowledged their fault, and repentance would have brought forth some fruit; as it is, they are satisfied with a vanity as empty as the wind — an example, he says, of the dissimulation that continually implicates men in new snares.

Jacob's own part he handles more carefully than the words allow. To indulge grief knowingly and voluntarily is as good as rebelling against God; but Calvin takes the refusal to be limited to the alleviation men could offer, nothing being more unreasonable than that a holy man who had borne the yoke of God all his life should now, like an unbroken horse, bite his bridle. He does not doubt Jacob still submitted to the Lord while rejecting human consolations, and thinks he chides his sons angrily besides, as if to upbraid them by declaring that he esteemed this one son above all the rest, desiring rather to lie dead with him than to enjoy the ten left him. The excess itself he will not excuse. A man so overwhelmed with sadness speaks of the grave as if the sons of God did not pass through death to a better life; and hence we learn the blindness of immoderate grief, which almost quenches the light of faith in the saints — as Job, greatly excelling in piety, yet mixed men with beasts in death once his grief oppressed him. The principal mitigation of sorrow is the consolation of the future life, to which whoever applies himself need not fear absorption by grief.

Yet Moses' design, on Calvin's reading, was not to condemn the father but to set a mark of infamy on the iron hardness reigning in his sons. They saw that if their father perished, consumed with grief, they would be the cause; they saw him already dying through their wickedness. If they could not heal the wound, why not at least attempt to alleviate the pain? They are exceedingly cruel, Calvin ends, in having so little care of their father's life that they would not drop one word in mitigation of his sorrow, when it was in their power.
36:
Gill distinguishes here what he had merged before: these were Medanites, sprung from Medan, a brother of Midian, distinct from the Midianites though dwelling near them and now in company with them and the Ishmaelites, all concerned in the sale, which is why it is ascribed now to one, now the other. Ellicott reads the Hebrew the same way and gives three chief interpretations of the buyer's name: two Coptic words meaning father of the king, a title equivalent to vizier; Gesenius's reading of it as the same name as Potipherah, consecrated to Ra the sun-god; and Canon Cook's father of the palace.

Whether he was a eunuch divides them. Gill says the word is sometimes so used but cannot mean it here, since Potiphar had a wife and, some say, a child; he was a chamberlain or other court officer. Ellicott offers two ways out: either the word had come to mean any palace officer, or Potiphar was chief of the eunuchs and so numbered among them. Calvin dismisses the question: he is called a eunuch not because he was one, but because among the Orientals it was usual to denote the satraps and princes of the court by that name. Clarke alone takes the literal sense and defends it. Lest it seem absurd that a eunuch should have a wife, he observes that in the east it is not uncommon, some keeping a whole seraglio though they appear to have no progeny — and discontent on that ground may have done as much for the unfaithfulness of Potiphar's wife as the motive commonly assigned her.

The title too is read three ways, all four noticing that the Hebrew says slaughterers. Gill takes it of cooks and butchers, of whom Potiphar was chief, or rather of executioners, having charge of prisoners and of putting them to death, like our sheriffs. Clarke calls chief of the butchers a most appropriate name for the guards of an eastern despot: if a man offend such a prince, the order to a life-guard is, go and bring me his head, obeyed at once, without judge, jury or law. Ellicott sets the versions against each other — the Septuagint understood slaughterers of animals for food and translated chief cook, the others the commander of the body-guard, who would execute condemned criminals — and settles it by the same title borne by Nebuzar-adan. Calvin, tracing the word from butchers to sacrificers to executioners, prefers prefect of the soldiers — not commander of the whole army, but holding the royal troops under his hand, an office his own day would have to join with that of prefect of the prison.

Two of them close the chapter, not the verse. Calvin calls it a sad spectacle that Joseph should be driven from one hand to another, no small indignity added to his former suffering that he was set to sale as a slave; yet the Lord did not cease to care for him, suffering the transfers so that it might at length appear he had come by celestial guidance to the dominion promised him in his dreams. Clarke ends with three. The history beginning here shows such wonders wrought by Divine Providence as cannot fail to confirm our faith. Joseph has often been considered a type of Christ, and Clarke rehearses the parallels while refusing to vouch for them: where the Spirit of God has not marked a direct resemblance, it is bold, if not dangerous, to call a man such a type. Envy he defines as pain felt, and malignity conceived, at the sight of excellence or happiness in another man — a man may envy his neighbour's wisdom, he says, though it gives him good counsel. And a house divided against itself cannot stand: parents should take heed that their own conduct be not the first cause of it, by exciting envy through undue partiality.
